I've got 6 mu on the North China Plain. The system here is simple and proven — winter wheat, then summer maize, same land, all year. That's what I do, that's what my neighbors do, and after five years I've gotten comfortable with the rhythm.

I'm not a traditional farmer who inherited land and methods. I came to this with a degree, I read extension materials, and I talk to the agronomists at the county station. My wife and oldest child both work off-farm, so the pressure isn't purely on what I grow — but I still want to maximize yield because the land is limited and inputs cost money.

**Wheat:** I'll plant in mid-October after I finish maize harvest and rotary-till to bury stubble. I use improved varieties — something like Jimai 22 or Kenong 199, which are well-adapted here and give consistent yield. I split my nitrogen: base fertilizer at seeding, topdress at jointing. I'll water three times — once before winter sets in, once at jointing, once at grain filling. I'm not going to irrigate heading unless we get an unusually dry spring; the well is there but electricity costs money. Two pesticide passes — one herbicide in early spring, one fungicide-insecticide before heading. I expect around 450 kg/mu.

**Maize:** Right after the combine clears the wheat in early June, I direct-seed maize into the stubble — no-tillage. This saves me time and cost, and the soil structure is better for it. I always use hybrid seed (Zhengdan 958 or Xianyu 335). Summer has more rain so I only irrigate twice — once at sowing if the soil is dry, once around tasseling if July is harsh. I topdress nitrogen at the V6 stage. Two pesticide applications: post-emergence herbicide, and one spray for corn borer in August. I expect around 550 kg/mu.
